config.alignedTo: The Nonconformance and Variance Processing procedure (draft, not yet released), EIA-649-1A, and GEIA-HB-649A. Checked 2026-09-28. The procedure is still a draft, and its title, numbering, and structure will change before release. For that reason the course never cites the procedure by identifier, section, or step number, and it never names the safety management system document. Each section is tagged below with the rule it restates, by name. When the procedure is released, walk this source map rule by rule and reconcile each tagged section. The four contract-tailoring items (minor delegation, DD Form 1694 and DI-SESS-80640, NCR form as the minor vehicle, records submitted) are taught on both branches and tested only on what holds either way. The course teaches the full EIA-649-1A major-classification list, because the procedure's CSA-acceptance example depends on the alternate-item criterion its own summary omits. Background boxes quote EIA-649-1A, GEIA-HB-649A, AS9131, and NAS9927 for context; no check, drill line, or exercise depends on them.

course.title: Nonconformance and Variance Training
course.subtitle: How a nonconforming part becomes a decision, how that decision becomes a controlled record, and where CM's authority starts and stops.
course.intro: Work through the sections in order. Each ends with a question that checks the point it made. Module 2 has a drill. The written exercises come at the end of each module. They are what {trainer} will actually read.

meta.v: CM engineers and CM specialists. No engineering background is assumed. Where the course uses a technical idea, it explains it.
None. Work the modules in order.
Allow about an hour for each module, plus the exercises.

keptExtra: When you are done, go to **Review and send**. It shows your scores, gathers every answer into one record, and gives you the ways to send it.

x: Nothing. The course stands alone. Where you need a definition from the standards, it is quoted in full on the page.
Boxes with a dashed border add context from the industry standards behind this process. Read them for understanding. No check question, drill line, or exercise depends on them.
The process is written to work across contracts. Four of its answers come from the contract. The course teaches both paths for each one, and checks only what holds on every contract.

course.closing: Enter your name in the header before you begin. It goes on the record you send.
exIntro: Write your reasoning, not just your conclusion. The reasoning is what is being assessed, and several of these have more than one defensible answer. Where a question turns on a fact you have not been given, **say so, and say what you would ask for and whom you would ask.** Recognizing the missing fact is part of the exercise.

glossary.d: An individual or enterprise that (1) commissions the engineering, design, manufacturing, production, or maintenance of a product; (2) is a prospective purchaser of the end products of a system or a portion thereof; (3) is a procurer of the product; (4) is a user or consumer of the product; or (5) is an obtainer of output service or product. *(EIA-649-1A)*
The party (e.g., DCMA) authorized by the Acquirer to disposition or concur on variances per contract.
Configuration of a product, at a specific point in time, which serves as a basis for defining change, for conducting verifications and for other management activities. *(EIA-649-1A)*
Categorization of a variance by the severity of the nonconformance's impact on the product and its requirements: critical, major, or minor.

A chartered board composed of technical and administrative representatives who recommend approval, defer with comments to be adjudicated, or disapproval of proposed engineering changes and variances to a configuration item's current approved and baselined configuration documentation. *(EIA-649-1A)*

A product or an aggregation of products (hardware, software, firmware, or documentation) that accomplishes an end-use function, is under separate configuration control and is designated for configuration management control. *(EIA-649-1A)*

A technical and management process, which establishes and maintains consistency between the product requirements, the product configuration information, and the product itself. It will identify, control, record, and verify. *(EIA-649-1A)*

The CM function that formalizes the recording and reporting of the established product configuration information (including historical information), the status of proposed changes, and the implementation of approved changes and changes occurring to product units due to operation and maintenance. *(EIA-649-1A)*
The part of a contract that lists the data items the supplier must deliver, each tied to a data item description.
The planned actions that remove the cause of a nonconformance and prevent it from happening again.
A document that defines the content and format of a contract deliverable. DI-SESS-80640 is the DID for a request for variance.
Defense Contract Management Agency. On many defense contracts it acts at the supplier's plant as the Acquirer's designated representative.
The Department of Defense form for a request for variance, used when the contract invokes it.

A designation, defining the product range e.g., serial numbers, block numbers, batch numbers, lot numbers, model, dates or event, at which a specific product configuration applies, a change is to be or has been affected, or to which a variance applies. *(EIA-649-1A)*

A proposed engineering change to the product and/or its configuration documentation, by which the change is described, justified, and submitted to a Configuration Approval Authority for approval/disapproval or deferral. *(EIA-649-1A)*
A variance requested before the item is produced, when the supplier knows in advance it must depart from the item's requirements.
A variance for a nonconformance discovered after an item is produced. Also called a production/procurement variance.

The formal examination of functional characteristics of a Configuration Item to verify that it met the requirements specified in its functional and allocated configuration documentation. *(EIA-649-1A)*
A formal examination of the actual (as-built) configuration of an item compared to its product configuration documentation. *(EIA-649-1A)*
The safety function's record of identified hazards and their status.

An item which (1) possesses comparable functional and physical characteristics as to be equivalent in performance, reliability and maintainability to another item of similar or identical purposes; and (2) is capable of being exchanged for the other item without selection for fit or performance, alteration of the items themselves, or adjoining items, except for adjustments. *(EIA-649-1A)*

A Supplier's multi-disciplined board, composed of personnel representing, at a minimum, quality (lead), engineering, and manufacturing/production representatives, identified by position, who determine and recommend approval or disapproval of proposed dispositions for nonconforming material or services (when such authority has been delegated to them), or who recommend submittal of ECPs or RFVs for Acquiring Activity disposition. *(EIA-649-1A)*
A condition of product or material that departs from approved product definition information or does not meet baseline requirements. The condition, not a document.
The record documenting an identified nonconformance. Not itself a variance.

Information that defines the product's requirements, documents the product attributes, including the process information and is the authoritative source for configuration management of the product. *(EIA-649-1A)*
Product released and later found nonconforming to contract or specification: a delivered use-as-is item, an escaped nonconformance, or a field-discovered defect.

A procedure which reduces but does not completely eliminate a nonconformance from a CI and which has been reviewed, concurred, and approved for use by the Acquirer. The characteristic after repair still does not completely conform. Unique configuration identification must be applied to repaired items. *(GEIA-HB-649A)*

The information by which a supplier requests permission to depart from product definition requirements for a specific unit, number of units, or time period, without baseline revision. It does not require the use of a form.
A procedure applied to a nonconformance that will completely eliminate it and result in a product that conforms completely to the drawings, specifications, or contract requirements. *(EIA-649-1A)*
An organization's formal system for managing safety risk. In this process it runs alongside as a safety overlay and consumes safety-relevant nonconformance and variance data.
The safety function's cycle of hazard identification, risk analysis, risk assessment, and risk control.
Disposition removing the nonconforming product from use.
Disposition accepting the nonconforming product without rework or repair, justified as not impacting approved requirements and interfaces.
Authorization for a nonconforming product to depart from baseline requirements for a specific unit, number of units, or period of time, without revising the product definition information.

modules.label: Module 1
modules.title: The words and the people
modules.sub: What a nonconformance is, what a variance is, and who owns which part of the decision

sections.title: A part that does not match its definition

body.x: Start with a part. A machined bracket comes off the mill. Its drawing puts a fastener hole 12.00 mm from edge A, plus or minus 0.10 mm. An inspector measures 12.40 mm.
The bracket does not match its definition.
Three questions follow at once. What happens to this bracket? Who decides? And what record proves the decision was made by the right people, for the right units, under the right authority?
This course teaches the process that answers those questions. The process runs from the moment Quality finds the problem to the moment the record is closed.

x.b: Something physical happens to it. It is reworked, repaired, used as it is, or scrapped.
Someone judges how severe the departure is. That judgment sets who must approve it.
The decision is identified, stored, submitted where required, and closed. It stays findable for the life of the product.

body.x: You work in CM. Some of you are engineers. You could read the drawing and judge the 0.40 mm yourself. Some of you are specialists. You may never open a drawing. This process asks the same thing of both of you.
Control the record. Do not judge the part.
body.sub: The technical decision belongs to a board of engineering, quality, and manufacturing. The record belongs to CM.

x: **Module 1** gives you the words and the people.
**Module 2** follows the part from discovery to disposition.
**Module 3** covers classification and who approves what.
**Module 4** covers the variance as a controlled record.
**Module 5** covers where CM's authority stops, how a record closes, and how safety data flows out.

check.q: In the bracket example, what does this process ask CM to do?
o: Control the record of the decision
Measure the hole again to confirm the finding
Decide whether the bracket can be used as it is
Decide how severe the 0.40 mm departure is
check.why: CM controls the record. Measuring belongs to Quality. Deciding what happens to the part, and how severe the departure is, belongs to the technical board. The rest of the course shows why the line sits there.

body.x: A departure only means something against a reference. The reference is the approved definition of the product.

For the bracket, the reference is its drawing at the released revision. For a circuit card, it might be a drawing plus a specification for the soldering process. For a purchased valve, it might be a supplier specification named in the purchase order. The contract can add requirements of its own.
The standards call this body of information **product definition information**. The definition is precise, so here it is in full.

x: Information that defines the product's requirements, documents the product attributes, including the process information and is the authoritative source for configuration management of the product.

body.x: Notice the words *authoritative source*. When the part and its definition disagree, the definition wins. The part is the thing that is wrong.
Product definition information is approved at a point in time. The approved set is a **baseline**. Changes and variances are measured against it.

x: Configuration of a product, at a specific point in time, which serves as a basis for defining change, for conducting verifications and for other management activities.

body.x: Some products get extra attention. They are designated **Configuration Items (CIs)**. A CI has its own identification, and often its own specification. When a nonconformance is recorded, the record names the affected CI or component. That ties the record to the right place in the product.
Keeping the product and its definition consistent is the purpose of configuration management.

x: CM is a technical and management process, which establishes and maintains consistency between the product requirements, the product configuration information, and the product itself. Configuration management process will identify, control, record, and verify the product requirements are met, the product configuration information is clear, complete, and accurate, and that the product itself is consistent with the product configuration information.

body.x: Four verbs carry that definition: **identify, control, record, verify.** Hold on to them. In this process, everything CM does is one of those four verbs. Judging a part is not one of them.

check.q: The bracket measures 12.40 mm. Its released drawing says 12.00 mm, plus or minus 0.10 mm. Which statement is correct?
o: The bracket departs from its product definition information, and the drawing is the authoritative source
The drawing should be revised to 12.40 mm so the bracket conforms
Whether it is a departure depends on whether the bracket still works
It is only a departure if the customer notices it
check.why: Product definition information is the authoritative source. The drawing says 12.00 ± 0.10 mm, so a bracket at 12.40 mm departs from it. Whether the bracket still works is a question for the disposition. It does not change the fact of the departure. Revising the drawing to match one bad part turns the logic upside down.

sections.title: Nonconformance: the condition and the record

body.x: The bracket's hole is 0.30 mm beyond its tolerance. That physical fact exists whether anyone writes it down or not.
The moment an inspector writes it down, a second thing exists: a record.
The process keeps these two things apart. It uses two terms.

x: A condition of product or material that departs from approved product definition information or does not meet baseline requirements. The condition, not a document.
The record documenting an identified nonconformance. Not itself a variance.

body.x: The nonconformance is the hole. The NCR is the paper, or the database entry, that says the hole is wrong.

The second definition ends with a warning. An NCR is not a variance. Opening an NCR authorizes nothing. It records that a problem exists. Whether the NCR ever leads to a variance is decided later, by a board you will meet in this module.
An NCR records a problem. It authorizes nothing.

check.q: An inspector opens an NCR on the bracket. What has the NCR done?
o: Recorded that a nonconformance exists
Authorized the bracket for delivery with the hole where it is
Created a variance for the bracket
Changed the drawing tolerance to match the bracket
check.why: An NCR documents an identified nonconformance. It is not a variance, so it authorizes nothing, and it changes no drawing. Whether a variance follows is decided later.

body.x: Suppose the team decides the bracket can be used with its hole where it is. The drawing still says 12.00 mm. Nobody wants to change the drawing. Every other bracket should still be made to 12.00 mm.
What the team needs is permission for this bracket to depart from the drawing. That permission is a **variance**.

x: Authorization for a nonconforming product to depart from baseline requirements for a specific unit, number of units, or period of time, without revising the product definition information.

body.x: Three limits are built into that definition.

x: It covers a nonconforming product.
It covers named units, or a named period of time. It does not cover everything built from now on.
It leaves the product definition information untouched. The drawing stays at 12.00 mm.

body.x: A change is different. A change revises the definition for every unit that follows. A variance leaves the definition alone and excuses specific units from it.

head: Variance
Change
x: What it alters
Nothing in the definition. It authorizes named units to depart.
The definition itself. The drawing or specification is revised.
Units covered
A specific unit, number of units, or period of time
Every unit built to the new revision
Bracket example
Serial 0112 is accepted with its hole at 12.40 mm.
The drawing tolerance is opened to plus or minus 0.50 mm.

body.x: The request that asks for a variance has its own name.

x: The information by which a supplier requests permission to depart from product definition requirements for a specific unit, number of units, or time period, without baseline revision. The standard explicitly states this does not require the use of a form.

body.x: Read the last sentence twice. An RFV is information. It is not a particular form. Module 4 puts that fact to work.

x: EIA-649-1A defines a variance as "an authorized temporary departure from the approved configuration documentation information for a specific number of units under the contract or contracts identified and that does not require revision of approved product configuration documentation." It adds that a variance "cannot be used to modify the configuration documentation information."

Older documents use two other names. A **deviation** was authorized before the item was built. A **waiver** was authorized after. EIA-649-1A lists both as former names for a variance. The Navy uses Departure From Specification.

check.q: Which statements are true of a variance? Choose all that apply.
o: It authorizes specific units, or a specific period of time, to depart from the baseline
It leaves the product definition information unchanged
It revises the drawing so later units conform
It must be submitted on a dedicated RFV form
check.why: A variance authorizes named units or a named period to depart, and it leaves the definition alone. Revising the drawing is a change, not a variance. The RFV is information, and the definition says it does not require a form.

body.x: A lot of 40 brackets was drilled on one setup. Inspection finds the hole out of position on serials 0108 through 0115. The other 32 brackets are good.
Which brackets should a variance cover? Only the eight that are wrong. That range is the variance's **effectivity**.

x: A designation, defining the product range e.g., serial numbers, block numbers, batch numbers, lot numbers, model, dates or event, at which a specific product configuration applies, a change is to be or has been affected, or to which a variance applies.

body.x: For a variance, effectivity names the units the variance applies to. The process sets one rule for it.
Effectivity is limited to as few units as possible.

The reason is traceability. Every unit inside the effectivity departs from its baseline. Every one of them must be tracked for the life of the product. A variance written for the whole lot of 40, when only eight serials are bad, puts 32 good parts under a departure they do not have.

Effectivity is handled three times. Quality captures the serial or lot data when it writes the NCR. The board that decides the part's fate confirms it. CM then maintains it in the record, still limited to as few units as possible.

x: GEIA-HB-649A adds that a variance intended for all subsequent units should be submitted as a request for change instead. A variance with open-ended effectivity is a change in disguise.

check.q: Serials 0108 through 0115 of a 40-piece lot have the hole out of position. What effectivity should the variance carry?
o: Serials 0108 through 0115
The whole lot of 40, so the record is simpler
All future brackets built on the same setup
No effectivity, because the part number is enough
check.why: Effectivity is limited to as few units as possible. Eight serials are bad, so the variance names those eight. The whole lot would put good parts under a departure. Future units would turn the variance into a change. A part number alone does not say which units depart.

body.x: Four parties act in this process. Each owns a different piece.

head: Party
Owns
x: Quality
Detecting, documenting, and segregating the nonconformance. Capturing effectivity and serial data. Verifying rework and corrective action.
Material Review Board (MRB)
Impact assessment. Disposition: rework, repair, use-as-is, or scrap. Classification: minor, major, or critical. For minors, direct submission.
CM
Configuration control of the variance as a record: identifier integrity, a valid status accounting record, effectivity control, recurrence and trend analysis, and closure.
Acquirer, or its designated representative
Disposition authority, according to the classification and the contract.

body.x: The Material Review Board
The MRB is a board, not a person. The standard defines it this way.

x: A Supplier's multi-disciplined board, composed of personnel representing, at a minimum, quality (lead), engineering, and manufacturing/production representatives, identified by position, who determine and recommend approval or disapproval of proposed dispositions for nonconforming material or services (when such authority has been delegated to them), or who recommend submittal of ECPs or RFVs for Acquiring Activity disposition.

body.x: Read the membership. Quality leads. Engineering and manufacturing sit with it. CM is not a defined member.
That fact matters later. It is one reason CM does not judge the technical questions the board decides.
The Acquirer and its representative

The **Acquirer** is the customer that buys the product. On defense contracts, the Acquirer often names a designated representative to act for it at the supplier's plant. The Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) is the common example.

x: The party (e.g., DCMA) authorized by the Acquirer to disposition or concur on variances per contract.

body.x: **Disposition**, used as a verb, means to make the formal decision on something. To disposition a variance is to approve or disapprove it.

check.q: Which party determines the disposition of the bracket: rework, repair, use as is, or scrap?
o: The Material Review Board
CM
The inspector who found the nonconformance
DCMA, on every nonconformance
check.why: Disposition belongs to the MRB. Quality found and documented the problem, and CM controls the record, but neither decides the part's fate. The Acquirer or its representative holds disposition authority only as the classification and contract direct.

sections.title: The split at the center of the process

body.x: One principle organizes the rest of this course. Here it is.
The MRB decides the technical fate of the part and its classification. CM owns the variance as a controlled configuration record.
body.sub: The tool carries the CM control, so neither delivery nor traceability depends on a CM person in the loop.

body.x: Take it one piece at a time.

**The technical fate.** Is the bracket reworked, repaired, used as is, or scrapped? How severe is the departure? These are engineering and quality judgments. The board with the engineering and quality members makes them.

**The controlled record.** Does the variance have one unique identifier? Is its effectivity captured? Is it stored where it can be found, reported, and trended for the life of the product? Is it closed when the reason for it ends? These are identify, control, record, and verify questions. CM owns them.

**The tool.** In this process, no CM person sits between the MRB and the customer. The NCR tool assigns the identifier and feeds the CM record system automatically. CM defines and polices those controls. CM does not hand-carry each record.
That does not shrink CM's job. It moves it. Modules 4 and 5 show exactly where it goes.

x.b: Disposition. Classification. Impact. The need for the variance, its cause, and the corrective action.
The identifier. Effectivity. The status accounting record. Recurrence and trends. Closure.

check.q: The MRB classifies a variance as minor. A CM engineer reads the record and believes the engineering call is wrong. Under the principle in this section, whose call is the classification?
o: The MRB's
The CM engineer's, because CM owns the record
Whoever reviews the record last
The inspector who found the nonconformance
check.why: The MRB decides the technical fate of the part and its classification. CM owns the record, not the severity judgment. Module 5 shows what CM can do when a record contradicts its own classification. Re-classifying is not one of those things.

exercises.title: Exercise 1: The hinge lot
exercises.scen: A lot of 25 hinges, part number 5520-118, reaches final inspection. Serials 0014, 0015, and 0019 have a pin bore below its minimum diameter. The other 22 hinges measure good. Quality opens one NCR. A production planner says: "Put the whole lot on a variance so the line keeps moving. Or just change the drawing so the small bore is legal."

parts.q: The planner treats the NCR as if it already allows the hinges to ship. Is it a variance? Explain what the NCR does and does not do.
parts.key: No. An NCR documents an identified nonconformance and is not itself a variance. It authorizes nothing. Whether a variance follows is decided later by the MRB.

parts.q: If a variance does follow, what effectivity should it carry? Why does that matter to CM?
parts.key: Serials 0014, 0015, and 0019 only. Effectivity is limited to as few units as possible. Every unit inside it departs from the baseline and must be tracked for life; putting 22 good hinges under the variance corrupts the record. CM maintains effectivity in the record.

parts.q: Compare the planner's two ideas: a variance, and a drawing change. Which one fits three bad hinges, and why?
parts.key: A variance authorizes named units to depart without revising the definition. A drawing change revises the definition for every unit that follows. Three bad hinges need a variance (if the MRB finds them usable), not a change to the drawing. Look for the words definition, named units, and future units.

exercises.title: Exercise 2: Whose call is it?
exercises.scen: You are a new CM specialist. A production lead walks up with the hinge NCR and says: "You're configuration management. Sign here that these three hinges are fine to use."

parts.q: Is this CM's decision? If not, whose is it, and who sits on that body?
parts.key: No. Disposition belongs to the MRB: quality (lead), engineering, and manufacturing or production, identified by position. CM is not a defined member.

parts.q: Name at least three things CM does own for this nonconformance once it leads to a variance.
parts.key: Any three of: the unique identifier and its integrity; effectivity control; the status accounting record and its validity; recurrence and trend analysis; closure. Strong answers tie these to identify, control, record, verify.

sections.title: Quality finds it and writes it down

body.x: Back to the lot of 40 brackets. The inspector has measured serials 0108 through 0115 and found the hole out of position. Here is what Quality does next.

x.b: Quality identifies a departure from approved product definition or baseline requirements and creates the NCR.
Quality physically separates the affected parts and tags them. Nobody can install or ship them by mistake.
Quality records the part number, the affected CI or component, the serial or lot effectivity, the quantity affected, the requirement or requirements departed from, and the as-found condition.

x.h: Let the tool assign and feed
x.b: The NCR tool assigns the unique variance record identifier. It feeds the CM status accounting system automatically.
Quality sends the NCR to the Material Review Board.

body.x: Here is what those facts look like for the brackets.

head: Field
Bracket NCR
x: Part number
Affected CI or component
Mounting bracket, landing light assembly
Effectivity
Serials 0108 through 0115
Quantity affected
Requirement departed from
Drawing 4471-203: hole position 12.00 ± 0.10 mm from edge A

Hole measured 12.35 to 12.42 mm from edge A

body.x: Look at the fourth step. The identifier comes from the tool the moment the NCR exists. Nobody from CM types it in later. Module 4 explains why that identifier must be the only identifier the record ever has.
An NCR is not yet a variance. Whether it becomes one is decided by the MRB.

check.q: Which of these does Quality capture on the NCR? Choose all that apply.
o: The serial or lot effectivity
The requirement departed from
The quantity affected
The classification: minor, major, or critical
The disposition: rework, repair, use-as-is, or scrap
check.why: Quality captures the facts of the finding: part number, affected CI or component, effectivity, quantity, the requirement departed from, and the as-found condition. Disposition and classification are decisions. The MRB makes them.

body.x: The NCR reaches the MRB. The board does one combined review. That review produces up to two outputs.

x.b: What happens to the part: rework, repair, use-as-is, or scrap. Every NCR gets one.
How severe the departure is: critical, major, or minor. Only needed when the disposition calls for a variance.

body.x: The words *up to two* matter. Every NCR gets a disposition. Not every NCR gets a classification. The next sections show which dispositions lead to a variance, and so to a classification.
The board also assesses impact. It asks what the departure does to the part, to the parts around it, and to how the product is used. That assessment feeds both outputs.

x: GEIA-HB-649A names the MRB and the change board as the two usual ways a supplier coordinates and evaluates a request for variance. It recommends a coordination checklist, so each affected department signs off that its impacts are addressed.

check.q: An NCR reaches the MRB. Which output does every NCR get?
o: A disposition
A classification
Both a disposition and a classification
Neither, until the customer responds

body.x: Four things can happen to a nonconforming part. Picture each one first.

x.b: A shaft is turned 0.06 mm oversize. The shop grinds it to the drawing dimension. It now meets the drawing in every respect.
A bracket hole is out of position. Engineering approves a bushing and a new hole. The bracket works, but it now has a bushing the drawing does not show.
A hole is 0.30 mm out of tolerance. Engineering shows the fastener still fits and the joint still carries its load. The bracket is used as it is.
A casting has a crack. It cannot be saved. It is removed from use.

body.x: Now the definitions. Two come from the standards word for word.

x: A procedure applied to a nonconformance that will completely eliminate it and result in a product that conforms completely to the drawings, specifications, or contract requirements. The Supplier must disclose that the rework occurred when outside the normal process to manufacture the part.

A procedure which reduces but does not completely eliminate a nonconformance from a CI and which has been reviewed, concurred, and approved for use by the Acquirer. The purpose of repair is to reduce the effect of the nonconformance. Repair is distinguished from rework in that the characteristic after repair still does not completely conform to the applicable drawings, specifications, or contract requirements. Unique configuration identification must be applied to repaired items.
*GEIA-HB-649A*
Disposition accepting the nonconforming product without rework or repair, justified as not impacting approved requirements and interfaces.
Disposition removing the nonconforming product from use.

The ground shaft does. That is rework. The bushed bracket does not. It works, but its drawing shows no bushing. That is repair.
Rework ends the nonconformance. Repair only reduces it.

Repair
Use-as-is
Scrap

What would a variance authorize for this shaft? Nothing. No departure is left to authorize.
That is the logic of rework. Rework completely eliminates the nonconformance. A part restored to full compliance has nothing to vary from the baseline.
So rework leaves the variance path. The NCR goes straight to verification. Quality verifies the part now conforms. The NCR closes. No variance is written. Nothing is submitted to the customer.

o: No variance is written, and the NCR closes after verification
A minor variance is written, because a nonconformance existed
A variance is written and sent to the customer
The MRB classifies it before the NCR can close

body.x: A cracked casting is scrapped. It is removed from use. It will never be delivered.
Does scrap need a variance? Usually not. A scrapped part is not delivered, so there is often no departure to authorize.

But some customers want scrap reported to them anyway. The contract decides. So the process says: record scrap as the contract requires, and write no request for variance unless the contract requires one.
Scrap: usually no variance. The contract decides.

When a contract does require a variance for scrap, that scrap takes the same road as repair and use-as-is. It is classified, and it goes forward as a variance. The course calls this **contractually required scrap**.

x: GEIA-HB-649A says that for scrap, variances "may, or may not be required, and is dependent on Acquirer requirements with the Supplier."

check.q: A casting is scrapped. The contract says nothing about variances for scrap. Is a request for variance required?
o: No. Record the scrap as the contract requires, with no RFV unless the contract requires one.
Yes. Every scrapped part needs a minor variance.
Yes. Scrap is always a major variance.
Only if CM decides the scrap should be reported
check.why: Scrap normally needs no variance, because the part is never delivered. The contract can require one. Here it does not, so no RFV is written.

body.x: Now the bushed bracket, and the bracket used with its hole where it is. Both will be delivered. Both still depart from the drawing.
A repair only reduces the nonconformance. The repaired part still does not fully conform. Use-as-is accepts the nonconformance outright. The part is delivered as it was found.
In both cases a noncompliant part is delivered or accepted. That takes an authorized variance. So repair and use-as-is go on to classification.

body.x: People often start with the wrong question. They ask, "Is it minor?" Then they decide from the answer whether a variance is needed.
That gets it backwards. Severity decides who approves a variance. It does not decide whether a variance exists.
The question is not "Is it minor?" The question is "Will a still-noncompliant part be delivered or accepted?"
body.sub: If yes, a variance is required and gets classified. If the part is made compliant, or never delivered, generally no variance.

body.x: Run the four dispositions through it.

x: **Rework.** The part is made compliant. Nothing noncompliant is delivered. No variance.
**Scrap.** The part is never delivered. No variance, unless the contract requires one.

**Use-as-is.** The part does not conform, and it is accepted. Variance.

body.x: Notice what the rule never asks. It never asks how small the departure is. A 0.01 mm departure used as is needs a variance. A gross defect that is scrapped normally does not.

A minor variance. Any defect needs one.

A variance only if the customer asks for one

The MRB confirms the effectivity Quality captured, limited to as few units as possible.

The cause and the corrective action look ahead. The variance excuses these eight brackets. The corrective action protects the next lot.

Not a variance, because nothing has been built yet

exercises.title: Exercise 1: The oversize bore
exercises.scen: Six cast housings, part number 3120-907, have a bore 0.08 mm oversize. The MRB weighs two options. Option 1: install a sleeve and re-machine the bore under an engineering-approved procedure. The drawing does not show a sleeve. Option 2: scrap the six housings and make new ones, which takes five weeks. The contract says nothing about scrap.

parts.q: For each option, name the disposition and say whether a variance is required. Use the trigger rule.
parts.key: Option 1 is repair: the housing still does not fully conform (sleeve not on drawing) and is delivered, so a variance is required. Option 2 is scrap: never delivered, and the contract is silent, so no variance. The answer must use the delivered-or-accepted test, not severity.

parts.q: If the MRB chooses option 1, what must it document beyond the disposition itself?
parts.key: Need statement (why ship rather than dispose), cause, recommended corrective action or CAP, confirmation of effectivity limited to as few units as possible, plus the classification. Strong answers mention that repair needs Acquirer review and approval.

parts.q: How will someone tell a repaired housing from an unrepaired one ten years from now?
parts.key: Repaired items receive unique configuration identification. Look for that point.

exercises.title: Exercise 2: "It's only a scratch"
exercises.scen: A supervisor finds a light scratch on a machined surface. The scratch is outside the drawing's surface-finish limit. The supervisor says: "It's tiny. It's minor. So we don't need a variance. Ship it."

parts.q: What is wrong with the supervisor's reasoning?
parts.key: Starts from severity. Severity decides who approves a variance, not whether one exists. If the part ships as it is, a noncompliant part is delivered: use-as-is, variance required.

parts.q: What question should be asked instead? What facts would you need to answer it?
parts.key: Will a still-noncompliant part be delivered or accepted? Need the MRB's disposition: rework to compliance (for example, refinish to the drawing), repair, use-as-is, or scrap. Good answers note CM does not make that disposition.

body.x: Two brackets are both used as is. One has a hole out of position on a cover that carries no load. The other has a hole out of position on a fitting in a flight control load path.
Both need a variance. They should not need the same approval.
Classification is how the process tells them apart.

x: Categorization of a variance by the severity of the nonconformance's impact on the product and its requirements.

body.x: Classification happens only for dispositions that need a variance: repair, use-as-is, and contractually required scrap. The MRB assigns it, in the same review that sets the disposition.
Classification drives authority. It is not set by who receives the record.
body.sub: Routing a record to DCMA does not make it minor.

body.x: That second line heads off a common shortcut. Someone sees a record going to DCMA. DCMA often handles minors. So they assume the record must be minor.
That reverses cause and effect. The class is judged from the departure's impact. The routing follows the class.

check.q: A record is being sent to DCMA. A reviewer concludes the variance must be minor, because DCMA is handling it. What is wrong with that conclusion?
o: The class is judged from the departure's impact. Routing follows the class, not the other way round.
Nothing. Anything sent to DCMA is minor by definition.
DCMA can only receive critical variances.
The reviewer should have classified it major, to be safe.
check.why: Classification drives authority. It is not set by who receives the record. The reviewer inferred the class from the routing, which reverses cause and effect.

body.x: Critical is the most severe class. It is defined by what the departure touches.

x: Use this classification when it is a departure from requirements affecting one or more of the following: i. Safety; ii. Human health; iii. Environment; iv. Security (local program or national).

body.x: Four words. If the departure affects any one of them, the variance is critical.

x: A fitting in a flight control load path that may not carry its rated load affects **safety**.
A seal material that can release a toxic vapor in a crew compartment affects **human health**.
A coating that releases a restricted substance when it is sanded affects the **environment**.
An encryption module built with an unapproved component affects **security**.

body.x: Critical variances are rare, and they should be. They also carry a consequence beyond approval. Module 5 shows that every critical variance feeds the safety management system.

x: GEIA-HB-649A cautions that critical variances should be avoided when at all possible, because of their extreme impact on the operation and maintenance of fielded units.

check.q: A departure in an avionics unit could let an unauthorized party read protected data. Which class fits?
o: Critical
Major
Minor
No class. It is a software issue, not a hardware departure.
check.why: Security, local program or national, is one of the four critical factors. A departure that could expose protected data affects security, so the variance is critical.

body.x: Major covers departures that affect how the item performs, fits, lasts, or is used, short of the critical factors. The process classifies against this list from the standard.

x: Use this classification when it is a departure from requirements affecting one or more of the following: i. Performance or operational limits; ii. Interchangeability, reliability, survivability, maintainability or durability of the item or its repair parts; iii. Structural strength; iv. Effective use or operation; v. Weight, moment of inertia, center of gravity; vi. Appearance; vii. Limits on product use or operation; viii. Temporary use of alternate items; ix. When the configuration documentation defining the requirements for the item classifies the departure from the requirement as major.

body.x: Some of these need translating if you do not work with drawings every day.

head: Factor
In plain terms
Example
x: Performance or operational limits
The item may not do its job across its full rated range.
A pump meets its flow at sea level but not at its rated altitude.
Interchangeability
The unit may no longer swap into place without selection, alteration, or modification.
A bracket's hole pattern no longer matches the standard mating part.
Reliability, survivability, maintainability, durability
The item may fail sooner, resist damage less, or be harder to service.
A bearing surface finish that shortens wear life.

The item may not carry its design load.
A fitting wall thinner than its minimum.

The item works, but not as effectively as specified.
A display that is readable but dimmer than specified.
Weight, moment of inertia, center of gravity
The item's mass or balance is off. That can shift the balance of whatever it is installed in.
A counterweight 40 grams heavy.
Appearance
How the item looks, where appearance is a requirement.
The wrong color on a visible cockpit panel.
Limits on product use or operation
The item can be used only under a restriction.
A valve cleared for fewer cycles than specified.
Temporary use of alternate items
A different part is substituted for the specified one.
Another vendor's fastener installed because the specified one is out of stock.
Classified major by the configuration documentation
The drawing or specification itself says this departure is major.
A drawing note flags a characteristic as major.

body.x: Two items catch people.
The first is **temporary use of alternate items**. A substitution can feel minor. The alternate part may be perfectly good. The criteria still make it major.
The second is **the configuration documentation**. When the drawing or specification classifies a departure, that classification governs.

check.q: The specified fastener is out of stock. Twelve units are built with a different vendor's fastener. Engineering says it performs identically. Which class do the criteria assign?
o: Major, because it is temporary use of an alternate item
Minor, because it performs identically
Critical, because fasteners hold structure
No class, because nothing departs from requirements
check.why: Temporary use of alternate items is a major factor. Identical performance does not remove it from the list. Nothing in the facts touches safety, health, environment, or security, so it is not critical.

body.x: Minor is defined by what is missing.

x: Use this classification when it consists of a departure that does not involve any of the factors listed for critical or major, or when the configuration documentation defining the requirements for the item classifies the departure from the requirement as minor.
Departures from the requirements that do not meet the definition of critical or major and are not classified in any configuration documentation (i.e., unlisted characteristic) are treated as minor.
*EIA-649-1A, note*

body.x: So minor is not a judgment that a departure is small. It is a finding that no critical factor and no major factor applies. A characteristic the documentation never classified defaults to minor.

That default is why screening matters. To call a departure minor honestly, the MRB must look at the critical factors and the major factors, and find none. Module 5 shows how CM checks that the screening was written down.

check.q: A wire marking sleeve uses an out-of-date label format. No critical or major factor applies. The drawings do not classify the label format. What class is the variance?
o: Minor
Major, because it departs from a drawing
No class, because the characteristic is unlisted
Critical
check.why: No critical or major factor applies, and the documentation does not classify the characteristic. An unlisted characteristic that meets neither definition is treated as minor.

body.x: Classification now decides authority. Start with minor, because the contract can set it up two ways.

The contract answers one question. Has the Acquirer delegated disposition of minor variances to the supplier's MRB? Or has it kept that authority with itself or its designated representative, such as DCMA?

Minor disposition retained by the Acquirer or DCMA

The MRB
The Acquirer's designated representative, such as DCMA

Nothing is required. The variance is recorded only.
The MRB submits the variance directly, as the controlled record.

Verifies the record and accepts it into status accounting
The same, in parallel with the submission
When the affected unit can be released
After CM's acceptance clears
The same

Either way, the affected unit is held until that acceptance clears.

Which format?

Many defense contracts invoke a set format for requests for variance. The common one is **DD Form 1694**, delivered under the data item description **DI-SESS-80640**. A data item description (DID) defines the content and format of a deliverable. The contract lists the DIDs that apply in its contract data requirements list (CDRL).

Whether DD Form 1694 and DI-SESS-80640 apply is a contract question. If they are invoked, CM submits the controlled RFV in that format. If they are not, CM submits the controlled RFV in whatever format the contract does call for.
The contract picks the format. The format never replaces the control.

Who submits

The MRB, if delegated. Otherwise the Acquirer's designated representative, such as DCMA.

exercises.title: Exercise 1: The substituted fastener
exercises.scen: Twelve actuators were built with an alternate vendor's fastener because the specified fastener was out of stock. The MRB proposes use-as-is and classifies the variance minor. Its record says: "Alternate fastener performs identically. No impact."

exercises.title: Exercise 2: Two programs, one minor

B: MRB submits directly to DCMA as the controlled record, DCMA dispositions; CM verifies and accepts into status accounting in parallel; unit released after acceptance clears.

sections.title: CM's control, carried by a tool

body.x: In many companies, a CM person receives each variance. That person gives it a number, types it into the record system, and carries it to the customer.
This process takes that person out of the delivery path. The NCR tool does the numbering and the feeding. The MRB submits minors directly.
That is allowed only if every control a CM person would have applied still happens. The process names four conditions. The model is compliant only if all four hold.

modules.label: Module 5
modules.title: Limits, closure, and safety
modules.sub: Where CM's authority stops, the check CM applies to minors, how a variance closes, and what feeds the safety management system

body.x: A CM engineer with twenty years in structures reads a variance. The MRB called it minor. The engineer is sure it is major. The engineer may even be right.
In this process, the CM engineer still does not re-classify it. The process gives six reasons.

x: **Classification is a technical severity judgment.** It weighs criteria such as safety, performance limits, interchangeability, and structural strength. Those are engineering and quality determinations, not record-control determinations.

**The standard gives that judgment to the MRB.** The MRB is the board of quality, engineering, and manufacturing. CM is not a defined member. Making CM a classifier, or a classification auditor, puts a function outside the board into a judgment reserved for the board.

**CM's defined scope excludes it.** CM's functions are identify, control, record, and verify. CM controls changes and variances as records and runs CSA. Variance approval authority sits with the engineering MRB manager or the Acquirer. CM is the release authority. Nothing grants CM authority over nonconformance severity.

**The defined dispute path is escalation to the Acquirer.** The standard's challenge runs between the supplier's MRB and the Acquirer. A CM audit layer would create a second, undefined internal classification authority. It would blur who owns the call.

**Classification controls who dispositions.** Classification sets the level of review and the approval authority. If CM re-classified, CM would decide which authority gets the variance. That encroaches on the MRB and the Acquirer.

**CM independence.** CM owns the record and controls customer submission. If CM also judged the class, the record-keeper would become a technical authority over its own records. That undermines the independence of the control function.

body.x: CM does not classify. CM does not disposition. CM does not override the MRB's classification.
body.sub: Classification disputes are escalated to the Acquirer for final decision.

body.x: What about the engineer who is sure? The next sections show the tools CM does have. They are narrower than re-classification. They are also real.

x: GEIA-HB-649A Table 6, a sample of approval authority levels, lists variance approval authority as the Engineering Material Review Board Manager and/or the Acquirer. It lists CM as release authority.

CM has no access to the NCR tool.
Only the customer may classify a variance.
CM staff cannot read drawings.
check.why: Classification sets the level of review and the approval authority, so a CM re-classification would let CM choose the authority. The reason is about roles, not skill. Even a CM engineer who can read the drawing does not classify.

body.x: None of this means CM looks away. CM audits. It audits a different thing.

x.b: Process and record compliance: a classification was assigned, the identifier and effectivity were captured, the record reached CSA. Product-to-documentation conformance, through configuration audits. Systemic patterns, through CSA trend analysis.
The technical correctness of the MRB's severity call on an individual variance.

body.x: Configuration audits compare the product with its documentation. The **functional configuration audit (FCA)** checks that an item met its functional requirements. The **physical configuration audit (PCA)** checks the as-built item against its product documentation. CM confirms these reconcile what was built to what is documented.
Trend analysis adds a systemic view. CM flags recurring nonconformances for consideration of an ECP or corrective action. That is pattern detection. It is not re-judging one MRB call.
CM audits whether the process was followed and the record is sound. It does not audit whether the engineering was right.

check.q: Which audit finding is within CM's scope?
o: A minor variance record has no classification assigned
Stress analysis shows the MRB should have classified a variance major
The engineering behind a repair procedure is weak
A use-as-is justification reaches the wrong engineering conclusion
check.why: A missing classification is a record compliance gap, which CM audits. The other three question the technical correctness of the MRB's judgment, which is outside CM's audit scope.

sections.title: The CSA acceptance check for minors

body.x: CM already touches every minor variance record at one point: when it accepts the record into CSA. The process puts a check there.

The check sits at CSA acceptance, not at customer submission. The MRB submits the minor directly to DCMA. CM's check runs in parallel, off DCMA's critical path. The customer is not kept waiting on CM.
The evidence CM requires
CM defines the minimum classification evidence a minor record must carry to be accepted into CSA:

x: the assigned classification;
the critical and major criteria that were screened; and
a basis statement saying why no critical or major factor applies.

body.x: At acceptance, CM verifies two things. The evidence is present. And the evidence is internally consistent with the documented facts in the record.
What CM does with what it finds

head: What CM finds
What CM does
x: The evidence is present and consistent.
Accepts the record into CSA. Verification passes.
Evidence is missing: no class, no criteria screen, or no basis statement.
Rejects the record and returns it for completeness.
The record's own facts show a critical or major criterion the classification does not address.
Rejects the record and escalates it: to the MRB, and, where the criteria indicate, to the Acquirer.

body.x: Look at the escalation row. CM does not declare the correct class. CM sends the call back to those who own it.
An example. A minor record says in its description: "Alternate vendor fastener installed. Specified part unavailable." Its basis statement says: "No critical or major factors apply."
The record contradicts itself. Temporary use of alternate items is a major factor. CM rejects and escalates. CM does not write "major" on it.
Every acceptance, rejection, and escalation is recorded in the CSA record, with its rationale.

o: Reject it and return it for completeness
Reject it and escalate it to the Acquirer
Accept it, because the class is assigned
Fill in the screened criteria and accept it
check.why: The screened criteria are required evidence. A record missing required evidence is rejected and returned for completeness. Escalation is for records whose own facts show an unaddressed critical or major criterion. CM does not supply the MRB's evidence itself.

body.x: A check with no consequence is a suggestion. This check has a consequence, and CM already holds it: configuration release authority.
A unit is not released for delivery until its minor variance record is accepted into CSA and verification has passed, or an escalation is dispositioned.
Walk serial 0112 through it. The MRB approves a minor use-as-is and submits it to DCMA. The same record enters CSA.

x: CM's check passes. The hold on serial 0112 clears.
CM rejects the record for completeness. Serial 0112 waits until the record is complete and accepted.
CM escalates the record. Serial 0112 waits until the escalation is dispositioned.

body.x: The hold covers minors whether the MRB dispositions them under delegation or submits them to DCMA. Either way, the unit waits for CSA acceptance.
CM records each decision, and the reason for it, in the CSA record. The decision is itself a record.

o: Not until the escalation is dispositioned
Yes, because DCMA has the record
Yes, if the MRB chair signs a release
Only after CM re-classifies the record
check.why: Configuration release is held until the record is accepted into CSA and verification passes, or the escalation is dispositioned. DCMA's receipt of the submission does not clear CM's hold.

body.x: Be exact about the check's reach. It catches two kinds of misclassification.

x: **The silent one.** The record carries no criteria screening at all.
**The self-contradicting one.** The record's own facts show a major factor, such as an alternate-item substitution, while the record still asserts minor.

body.x: It does not catch the third kind: the **competent-but-wrong** classification. The record is complete. It screens every criterion. Its basis statement agrees with its facts. And the engineering judgment behind it is wrong.
Finding that error takes engineering severity judgment. That judgment is the MRB's responsibility. It is outside CM's scope.
CM's check covers completeness and internal consistency. It is not engineering validation of the severity judgment.
body.sub: State this limit wherever the check is invoked, so CM is not assigned liability it cannot discharge.

body.x: This matters for your own protection. Suppose an auditor asks whether CM validated a classification. The true answer is: CM verified that the record was complete and consistent. CM did not validate the engineering, and could not.
The same limit applies to CM audits in general. CM's audit scope is process and record compliance and product-to-documentation conformance. It is not the technical correctness of the severity call.

check.q: A minor record was complete and consistent, and CM accepted it. Later, stress analysis shows the part should have been major. Did the CM check fail?
o: No. A competent-but-wrong classification is outside what the check can detect.
Yes. CM should have validated the engineering.
Yes. CM should escalate every minor.
No, because DCMA approved it.
check.why: The check covers completeness and internal consistency. A complete, consistent record with a wrong engineering judgment is the competent-but-wrong case, which only engineering severity judgment can find. That judgment belongs to the MRB.

body.x: Once a variance is dispositioned, it is recorded in CSA: its type, description, impact, corrective-action criteria, the action taken to prevent recurrence, and cost or consideration where applicable.
Now bracket 4471-203 comes back. Same hole, out of position again, next lot. The first variance's corrective action did not work.
CM watches for exactly this.

x: **CM flags recurring variances on the same part.**
**A recurring minor needs Acquirer approval before it is resubmitted.** CM ensures it is not resubmitted without that approval.
**Recurring engineering variances are evaluated for an ECP.** If the same departure keeps being requested, the requirement itself may need to change. CM ensures that evaluation happens.
**CM runs CSA trend analysis** to detect recurring nonconformances and report problems.

**CM reports recurring CSA-acceptance rejections as a process trend.** Suppose minor records for part substitutions keep being rejected. That pattern points at the process, not at one record. CM reports it for corrective action.

GEIA-HB-649A: a recurring variance "indicates that the corrective action was insufficient, not instituted or verified." When the technical requirements are too stringent, a request for change should be initiated.
EIA-649-1A limits an RFV to its documented effectivity, which must be less than or equal to the remaining contract period. An RFV applies only to the contract under which it is submitted.

check.q: Bracket 4471-203 needs a second minor variance for the same nonconformance. What must happen before it is resubmitted?
o: Acquirer approval
CM re-classifies it major
Nothing. Minors can be resubmitted freely.
An ECP must be approved first
check.why: A recurring minor needs Acquirer approval before resubmission. An ECP evaluation applies to recurring engineering variances, and CM never re-classifies.

body.x: Quality and the MRB drive corrective action. Rework is verified to conformance, and the NCR closes with no variance. For repair and use-as-is, the corrective action is executed, and the cause is investigated and corrected.
CM closes the variance. There are two ways to close one.

x.h: The product is brought into compliance
x.b: For example, compliant parts are later installed in the affected units.

x.h: An approved ECP revises the baseline
x.b: The requirement or design changes permanently. That eliminates the basis for the variance.

body.x: A variance does not close because the parts shipped, or because time passed. It closes on verification of one of those two things.

After closure, the record stays. CM retains closed variance records in CSA for the product life cycle, with full historical traceability. Serial 0112 may fly for thirty years. Its variance record must be findable for all thirty.

check.q: Put the life of a use-as-is variance in order.
o: Quality opens the NCR and segregates the part
The MRB dispositions it use-as-is and classifies it
The variance is recorded in CSA and submitted as the contract requires
Corrective action is executed and verified
CM closes the variance and retains the record
check.why: Quality finds and records. The MRB decides. The record enters CSA and goes where the contract sends it. Corrective action follows. CM closes on verification and keeps the record for the life of the product.

sections.title: The safety management system: what feeds it

body.x: A safety management system runs alongside this process. It is a safety overlay. It does not change variance disposition authority, classification, or the roles of CM and the MRB.

A quality management system is foundational to a safety management system. That makes the NCR and variance process an upstream data source. The safety management system consumes the safety-relevant part of what this process produces.
One more term first.

x: Product released and later found nonconforming to contract or specification: a delivered use-as-is item, an escaped nonconformance, or a field-discovered defect.

body.x: A safety-relevance screen runs in parallel with disposition. Quality and the MRB apply it. Four kinds of item feed the safety management system's hazard log and occurrence reporting, whatever the variance outcome.

x.b: By definition they affect safety, health, environment, or security. They are mandatory input to hazard identification.

Delivered use-as-is items, escaped nonconformances, and field or in-service defects. They are subject to occurrence reporting. A production organization also communicates safety-significant escapes to the design organization.
No variance results. Nothing goes to the customer. The defect may still carry hazard or trend information the hazard log should capture.
A trend signal for hazard identification. This is in addition to CM's recurrence and ECP check.

x: The quality escape concept comes from AS9131, the aerospace standard for nonconformance data definition and documentation. The duty to communicate safety-significant escapes from a production organization to the design organization comes from NAS9927, an aerospace industry standard for safety management systems.

check.q: A part with a safety-relevant defect is reworked to full compliance. No variance results. Does it feed the safety management system?
o: Yes. A safety-relevant nonconformance feeds it even when rework leaves no variance.
No. Only variances feed it.
No. Nothing reworked is reported anywhere.
Only if the customer asks for it.
check.why: The safety feed is independent of the variance outcome. A safety-relevant nonconformance reworked to compliance can still carry hazard or trend information, so it feeds the hazard log.

sections.title: The safety interface: how it works and where it stops

body.x: Three rules shape the interface.

x: **Parallel, not gated.** The safety feed is independent of classification and disposition. A reworked part that raised no variance can still be a safety item. A minor variance is not automatically a safety item.

**The flow.** Quality and the MRB flag safety relevance. The safety function logs the item in the hazard log and runs safety risk management: hazard identification, risk analysis, risk assessment, and risk control. CSA supplies trend and recurrence data. Safety-significant escapes flow to the design organization for continued operational safety.

**Ownership.** Quality, the MRB, and CM own the nonconformance and the variance. The safety function owns the hazard log, safety risk management, occurrence reporting, and design-organization feedback. The interface is a data feed, not a merger.

body.x: Where it stops

x: The safety management system does not change who classifies variances, the classification criteria, or the split between the MRB and CM. It adds a parallel safety obligation. Nothing more.
The safety feed supplements the CM and quality records. It does not replace them.
Not every nonconformance is a hazard. The screen filters for safety relevance. It is not a requirement to route every NCR into the safety management system.

body.x: CM's two safety duties

x: CM makes variance and nonconformance trend data available to the safety function for hazard identification.
CM ensures critical-classified variances and quality escapes are visible to the safety function. For production organizations, CM ensures they are routed for design-organization feedback.

check.q: Which statements about the safety interface are true? Choose all that apply.
o: A minor variance is not automatically a safety item
CM makes trend data available to the safety function
Every NCR must be routed into the safety management system
The safety function can re-classify a variance
check.why: The feed is parallel and filtered for safety relevance, so a minor is not automatically a safety item and not every NCR goes in. CM supplies trend data. The safety management system changes nothing about who classifies.

body.x: Here is everything this process asks of CM, in one place. Every line was taught in an earlier section.

head: Area
CM shall
x: Process ownership

Document the process in the CM plan or a referenced CM procedure. Maintain the configuration-control process that receives, identifies, and processes RFVs. The CM manager defines the CSA rigor the customer and contract call for.
Identifier and record control

Ensure each variance has a unique identifier, segregated from other change documents. Ensure the tool's identifier is the single identifier of record. Ensure it is assigned, and the record controlled, before release to the customer. Recognize the NCR form as the RFV when the customer agreed and the form carries full content.
CSA capture
Capture every variance at disposition. Validate required fields, classification, and effectivity. Track the status of corrective actions. Maintain effectivity, limited to as few units as possible.
The minor check

Define the minimum classification evidence. Verify it at acceptance. Reject and return incomplete records. Escalate records whose facts show an unaddressed critical or major criterion. Hold release. Record every decision and its rationale.
Submission control
Release only the controlled, identified record. Submit majors and criticals in the contract's format. Apply the check and the hold to minors the MRB submits.
Recurrence and trend

Run trend analysis. Flag recurring variances, and keep recurring minors from resubmission without Acquirer approval. See that recurring engineering variances are evaluated for an ECP. Report recurring acceptance rejections as a process trend.
Closure and retention
Track each variance to closure. Retain closed records for the product life cycle.
Safety interface
Make trend data available. Make critical variances and quality escapes visible, and route them for design-organization feedback where applicable.

head: CM shall not
x: Classify variances.
Disposition nonconforming material.
Re-adjudicate or override MRB classifications. Classification disputes are escalated to the Acquirer.
Treat its acceptance check as engineering validation. The check covers completeness and internal consistency only.
Audit the technical correctness of the severity call. CM's audit scope is process and record compliance and product-to-documentation conformance.

body.x: CM keeps the record true. The MRB keeps the judgment sound. The Acquirer settles what they cannot.

check.q: Which of these are CM obligations in this process? Choose all that apply.
o: Hold release of a unit until its minor record is accepted into CSA, or its escalation is dispositioned
Retain closed variance records for the product life cycle
Report recurring CSA-acceptance rejections as a process trend
Validate the engineering behind each minor classification
Decide the disposition of scrap when the contract is silent
check.why: The release hold, life-cycle retention, and trend reporting are CM duties. Validating engineering is outside CM's scope, and dispositioning material belongs to the MRB.

exercises.title: Exercise 1: The substitution at the check
exercises.scen: A minor variance record arrives in CSA. It reads: "Specified connector unavailable. Alternate connector from approved vendor list installed on serials 0201 through 0204. Classification: minor. Basis: no critical or major factor applies." The MRB submitted it to DCMA yesterday.

parts.q: What does CM do at CSA acceptance? Why?
parts.key: Reject and escalate: to the MRB, and where the criteria indicate, the Acquirer. The record's own facts (alternate item) show a major criterion (temporary use of alternate items) the minor classification does not address. It is self-contradicting.

parts.q: What happens to serials 0201 through 0204?
parts.key: Configuration release is held until the escalation is dispositioned. DCMA having the submission does not clear the hold.

parts.q: What does CM not do here? Why not?
parts.key: CM does not re-classify or write major on the record; it does not declare the correct class. Reasons: classification is the MRB's technical judgment; disputes go to the Acquirer; CM re-classifying would let CM choose the approval authority; independence of the record function.

exercises.title: Exercise 2: The auditor's question
exercises.scen: Six months after a minor variance was accepted into CSA, an engineering review finds the part should have been classified major. An auditor asks you: "Did CM verify this classification?" The record, as accepted, was complete and internally consistent.

parts.q: How do you answer the auditor?
parts.key: CM verified the record was complete (classification, criteria screened, basis statement) and internally consistent with its documented facts. CM did not validate the engineering severity judgment and is not scoped to. This is the competent-but-wrong case, the MRB's responsibility.

parts.q: Which kinds of misclassification would CM's check have caught?
parts.key: The silent one (no criteria screening) and the self-contradicting one (facts show a major or critical factor while the record asserts minor).

parts.q: If similar misclassifications keep appearing, what can CM legitimately do?
parts.key: Trend analysis: report recurring CSA-acceptance rejections or recurring problems as a process trend for corrective action. Not an individual re-classification.

exercises.title: Exercise 3: The cracked clamp
exercises.scen: During assembly, a fuel-line clamp is found cracked. The cracked clamp is removed and a conforming clamp is installed. The assembly now meets its drawing. Quality and the MRB judge the defect safety relevant.

parts.q: Is a variance required? Does anything go to the customer?
parts.key: No variance: rework to compliance (the assembly now fully conforms). Nothing goes to the customer, unless the contract requires otherwise.

parts.q: Does the finding feed the safety management system? Who flags it, and who logs it?
parts.key: Yes: safety-relevant nonconformances reworked to compliance feed it, independent of variance outcome. Quality and the MRB flag safety relevance. The safety function logs it in the hazard log and runs safety risk management.

parts.q: Cracked clamps show up on three lots this year. What does CM do with that?
parts.key: CSA trend analysis detects the recurring nonconformance and reports the problem; CM makes the trend data available to the safety function for hazard identification. Recurring nonconformances are also a trend signal for the safety management system.
